head.citation-title: Influences of the pile loads on the dynamic interaction between soft clay foundations and piles: A dynamic centrifuge study
head.abstracts: © 2026 Elsevier LtdNegative skin friction (NSF) plays a crucial role in the performance of piles in soft clay during earthquakes. However, the influence of the load at the pile top on the frictional resistance has not been extensively investigated. Existing design methods rarely quantify this influence and may often lead to considerable overestimations. To quantitatively assess this influence, in the present study a dynamic centrifuge test was conducted at 50 g on two model pile groups with identical configurations under different loads at the pile top. The measured responses included pile strains, soil accelerations, and pile–soil displacements, from which the bending moment, NSF, and soil resistance were derived. The results demonstrate that doubling the load at the pile top significantly reduces both the maximum pile bending moment by 7% and the lateral soil resistance by 33%. Moreover, a doubled load at the pile top, by increasing the pile settlement and thereby reducing the relative soil–pile displacement, significantly reduces the development of NSF along the pile shaft by 21%∼70% across the upper, middle, and lower pile sections. A key finding, contrasting sharply with static empirical estimates, is that the seismic NSF neutral depth reaches 0.81∼0.83 of the thickness of the compressible soil layer, markedly deeper than the empirically estimation of 0.5∼0.6 of the soil thickness. A preliminary predictive method for the maximum NSF is proposed based on this mechanistic insight, which explicitly incorporates the effect of the top pile load. This estimation method aims to provide a quantitative framework for understanding the pivotal role of the load at the pile top in the development of seismic NSF. Overall the present study offers clarified design parameters and an improved analytical perspective, potentially contributing to the advancement of seismic safety for pile foundations in soft clays.

coredata.dc:description: Negative skin friction (NSF) plays a crucial role in the performance of piles in soft clay during earthquakes. However, the influence of the load at the pile top on the frictional resistance has not been extensively investigated. Existing design methods rarely quantify this influence and may often lead to considerable overestimations. To quantitatively assess this influence, in the present study a dynamic centrifuge test was conducted at 50 g on two model pile groups with identical configurations under different loads at the pile top. The measured responses included pile strains, soil accelerations, and pile–soil displacements, from which the bending moment, NSF, and soil resistance were derived. The results demonstrate that doubling the load at the pile top significantly reduces both the maximum pile bending moment by 7% and the lateral soil resistance by 33%. Moreover, a doubled load at the pile top, by increasing the pile settlement and thereby reducing the relative soil–pile displacement, significantly reduces the development of NSF along the pile shaft by 21%∼70% across the upper, middle, and lower pile sections. A key finding, contrasting sharply with static empirical estimates, is that the seismic NSF neutral depth reaches 0.81∼0.83 of the thickness of the compressible soil layer, markedly deeper than the empirically estimation of 0.5∼0.6 of the soil thickness. A preliminary predictive method for the maximum NSF is proposed based on this mechanistic insight, which explicitly incorporates the effect of the top pile load. This estimation method aims to provide a quantitative framework for understanding the pivotal role of the load at the pile top in the development of seismic NSF. Overall the present study offers clarified design parameters and an improved analytical perspective, potentially contributing to the advancement of seismic safety for pile foundations in soft clays.
coredata.dc:title: Influences of the pile loads on the dynamic interaction between soft clay foundations and piles: A dynamic centrifuge study
